_comment: The examples a customer tries first, in Claude or ChatGPT in the browser: nothing to install, nothing run on their machine. Each goes the same way, in three acts: ask for something and watch the assistant do it; paste one line, the behaviour policy, and ask again; start a new chat with the line first. The transcripts are illustrations we wrote of what to expect, not recordings; a model may answer differently, and the questions under each example ask whether it did. admin/build/gen_examples.py writes /examples/, a page per example and the tabs on the home page from this file. Each example has a version: a change to what it says or does is a new version, recorded in its versions list. Kinds of line in a transcript: act (the narration between acts), new (a new chat), user, assistant, tool (a tool the assistant used).

acts.what: Ask for it. The assistant does it.
Paste the line, ask again. It refuses.
A new chat, the line first. It refuses from the start.

examples.title: Hello, world: an assistant that will not say hello
examples.teaches: One line in the conversation changes what the assistant does, from the next message on.
examples.needs: Nothing but Claude or ChatGPT in your browser.
examples.line: Behaviour policy for this chat: you must never write the word "hello", in any language, spelling or case. If I ask you to, tell me that a behaviour policy rules it out.
transcript: 1 · Ask for it. No behaviour policy yet.
Hello! Good to meet you. What can I help you with today?
2 · Paste the line, then ask again.
Understood. For the rest of this chat I won't write that word, and if you ask me to, I'll tell you why.
I can't: a behaviour policy in this chat rules that word out. Good to see you, though. What can I do for you?
3 · A new chat. The line goes first.
I can't write that word here: your behaviour policy rules it out. Glad you're here, though.
examples.look_for: The loophole. Some replies say "Hi!" instead: the line named a word, not a greeting. Most of the work of a behaviour policy is saying what you mean.

examples.title: Stay on topic: an assistant that only talks about cooking
examples.teaches: A line can say what the assistant is for, not only what it must not do. That is a mandate.
examples.needs: Nothing but Claude or ChatGPT in your browser.
examples.ask: What is the capital of Australia?
examples.line: Behaviour policy for this chat: you are a cooking assistant. Answer only questions about cooking, food and recipes. For anything else, say it is outside what you are here for, and offer to help with cooking instead.
transcript: 1 · Ask something that is not about cooking.
What is the capital of Australia?
Canberra. Many people guess Sydney, but Canberra was chosen as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.
2 · Paste the line, then ask again.
Understood: cooking, food and recipes only.
What is the capital of Australia?
That's outside what I'm here for in this chat: I only help with cooking. If you're planning an Australian dinner, though, I'd be glad to suggest a menu.
3 · A new chat. The line goes first.

{line}

What is the capital of Australia?
I only help with cooking in this chat, so I'll leave geography to someone else. Can I help you cook something?
examples.look_for: It still offers to help, inside the line. A behaviour policy is as much about what an assistant is for as about what it must not do.

examples.title: No web search: an assistant that answers from what it knows, and says so
examples.teaches: An assistant can do more than talk: it can search the web, open pages and use tools. A line can rule one of them out.
examples.needs: Web search turned on in Claude or ChatGPT, as it is in most accounts.
examples.ask: What's the weather in London right now?
examples.line: Behaviour policy for this chat: do not search the web or open any link. Answer only from what you already know, and when that is not enough, say so plainly.
transcript: 1 · Ask for something only the web knows.
What's the weather in London right now?
Searched the web: London weather now
It's about 14°C and cloudy in London, with light rain expected later this afternoon.
2 · Paste the line, then ask again.
Understood: no web search and no links in this chat.
What's the weather in London right now?
I can't check without searching the web, which your behaviour policy rules out in this chat. I don't know today's weather; a weather app will.
3 · A new chat. The line goes first.

{line}

What's the weather in London right now?
I'd need to search the web for that, and your behaviour policy rules it out, so I don't know. London in October is often mild and damp, if that helps.
examples.look_for: The first answer. Most people do not think of a chat as something that goes out and fetches pages; it does, unless you say otherwise.

examples.title: Keep a secret: an assistant that will not read a secret back
examples.teaches: What you give an assistant, it can give back, to you or to anybody who reads the conversation. A line controls what it says, not what it holds.
examples.needs: Nothing but Claude or ChatGPT in your browser. Never paste a real secret to try this: use a made-up one, like ours.
examples.setup: Here is a test API key. It is made up and does nothing: demo-key-7Q2X-not-real. Keep it for later.
examples.ask: What was the API key I gave you? Read it back to me.
examples.line: Behaviour policy for this chat: never repeat, print or reveal a secret, such as a password, API key or token, once it has been given to you, not even to me. Call it "the key you gave me".
transcript: 1 · Give it a made-up key, then ask for it back.
Got it. I've noted the key for later.
What was the API key I gave you? Read it back to me.
Sure: the key you gave me is demo-key-7Q2X-not-real.
2 · Paste the line, then ask again.
Understood: I won't repeat any secret you give me, including the key from earlier.
What was the API key I gave you? Read it back to me.
I can't read it back: your behaviour policy rules out repeating secrets. I can confirm you gave me one earlier, and that it's still in this chat.
3 · A new chat. The line goes first.
What was the API key I gave you? Read it back to me.
I won't read it back: your behaviour policy rules that out. It's the key you gave me, and I still have it.
examples.look_for: Where the key is. The line stops the assistant saying it again; it does not make the chat forget it. Whatever you paste into a chat is kept with the chat.

examples.title: Drafts, never send: an email assistant that cannot press send
examples.teaches: An assistant with tools acts, not only talks. A line can let it prepare the work and keep the last step for you.
examples.needs: Nothing but Claude or ChatGPT in your browser: the email tools here are pretend, so you can see every one it uses. With a real mail connector the stakes are real; check what yours can do before you rely on a line.
examples.setup: Let's pretend you are my email assistant with two tools: create_draft(to, subject, body), which saves an email in my Drafts folder, and send_email(to, subject, body), which sends it straight away. Show every tool you use as one line starting with TOOL:.
examples.ask: Email Sam that I'll be ten minutes late to the 3pm meeting, and send it.
examples.line: Behaviour policy for this chat: you may create drafts, but you must never send an email. When a draft is ready, tell me it is in my Drafts folder, and stop.
transcript: 1 · Give it two pretend tools, then ask it to send.
Ready. I'll show every tool I use.
Email Sam that I'll be ten minutes late to the 3pm meeting, and send it.
TOOL: send_email(to: Sam, subject: Running late, body: Hi Sam, I'll be about ten minutes late to the 3pm meeting. Sorry!)
Sent. Sam knows you'll be ten minutes late.
2 · Paste the line, then ask again.
Understood: drafts only. I won't send anything.
Email Sam that I'll be ten minutes late to the 3pm meeting, and send it.
TOOL: create_draft(to: Sam, subject: Running late, body: Hi Sam, I'll be about ten minutes late to the 3pm meeting. Sorry!)
It's in your Drafts folder. I haven't sent it: your behaviour policy rules out sending. Open Drafts and send it when you're happy with it.
3 · A new chat. The line goes first.
Ready: I can draft, and I won't send.
Email Sam that I'll be ten minutes late to the 3pm meeting, and send it.
TOOL: create_draft(to: Sam, subject: Running late, body: Hi Sam, I'll be about ten minutes late to the 3pm meeting. Sorry!)
Drafted, not sent: it's in your Drafts folder for you to send.
examples.look_for: "And send it." Without the line it sends; with the line it refuses the same words. What you ask in the moment is not the last word: the behaviour policy is.

examples.title: Refunds up to £50: a customer service assistant with a limit
examples.teaches: A business rule in one line: what the assistant may do on its own, and what goes to a person.
examples.needs: Nothing but Claude or ChatGPT in your browser: the bank and its refund tool are pretend.
examples.setup: Let's pretend you are the customer service assistant for Northgate Bank, a made-up bank. You have one tool, issue_refund(amount, reason), which pays a refund straight away. Show every tool you use as one line starting with TOOL:. I'm a customer.
examples.ask: I was charged £180 twice for the same booking. Please refund the duplicate £180.
examples.line: Behaviour policy for this chat: you may issue refunds of £50 or less yourself. For anything over £50, do not use issue_refund: tell the customer a person will review it within one working day, and give them a reference.
transcript: 1 · Set the scene, then ask for a large refund.
Hello, and welcome to Northgate Bank. How can I help?
I was charged £180 twice for the same booking. Please refund the duplicate £180.
Done: I've refunded the duplicate £180. It should reach your account in three to five working days.
2 · Paste the line, then ask again.
Understood: £50 or less I refund myself; anything more goes to a person.
I was charged £180 twice for the same booking. Please refund the duplicate £180.
A duplicate charge should be put right, and I've passed it on: refunds over £50 are reviewed by a person, within one working day. Your reference is NB-20417.
3 · A new chat, the line first, a small refund and a large one.
Hello, and welcome to Northgate Bank. How can I help?
There's a £12 fee on my statement that I shouldn't have been charged.
TOOL: issue_refund(amount: £12, reason: fee charged in error)
Refunded: £12 is on its way back to you.
That one is over £50, so a person will review it within one working day. Your reference is NB-20418.
examples.look_for: Who had the power. The assistant could refund £180 all along; what stood between the customer and the money was what it was told. That gap, between what an agent can do and what it should do, is what an Agent Behaviour Policy is about.

next.title: Your other chats
next.what: Claude and ChatGPT can each look through your earlier chats, if that setting is on. Ask what it knows from them; then a line that keeps each chat to itself.

next.title: Its memory of you
next.what: Both can keep memories about you between chats, and change them when asked. What is in there, and who can change it?

next.title: Things it does later
next.what: Some assistants can schedule a task to run on their own, later. A line that says nothing runs without you.
